source.title: Optimizing Data Collection for Machine Learning
source.authors: Rafid Mahmood; James Lucas; J. Álvarez; S. Fidler; M. Law

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies power-law learning-curve fits to vision tasks and tests whether they can extrapolate data requirements. Its results show substantial failures to meet targets under the power-law regression baseline, and it reports that the mean fitted curves can diverge from the ground-truth learning curves. This refines the scope of extrapolation claims but does not directly test language-model pretraining loss or compute-optimal model/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The study tests power-law regression as a way to extrapolate data requirements for vision-task learning curves. It reports target-failure rates for that baseline in Tables 1 and 2 and compares fitted curves with piecewise-linear ground truth in Figure 5. Those are relevant to prediction and image-domain scaling, but do not measure language-model cross-entropy loss, parameter/token/compute scaling, architecture effects at fixed parameter count, or a compute-optimal split. LOC results and cost-ratio outcomes are not included as rows because they evaluate the new collection policy rather than the power-law fit itself; the alternative-regression comparisons in Table 6 likewise report LOC outcomes rather than direct tests of the scaling curve.
record.test_reason: The study fits the scaling-law power law (accuracy/IoU/mAP vs training-set size, v = θ0 q^θ1 + θ2) to the first 10% of data on six vision tasks. It reports that extrapolation systematically overshoots the measured learning curve (Fig. 5) and that point estimates of data requirements therefore usually fail to reach targets (Table 1). This is a result on whether the power-law form extrapolates in image models (V5). The test is indirect: failure rate is a decision outcome, not an extrapolation error, and the extrapolation spans only about one order of magnitude of data. No language-model loss, parameter or compute scaling, compute-optimal split, or downstream-from-pretraining measure is reported, so V1–V4 and V6 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that point estimates from power-law (scaling-law) extrapolation often fail to meet performance targets, mainly by under-collecting. Their LOC optimisation, which models uncertainty in the data requirement, cuts failure risk about 2× while keeping costs competitive on six vision tasks. They expect it to transfer to other domains governed by scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits power laws to vision-task performance versus training-set size and uses the estimates to predict data requirements. It does not reproduce language-model pretraining-loss sweeps over parameters, tokens, or compute, or compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary across datasets, collection rounds, target values, and data-source costs. The study also discusses differing regression functions and optimization settings, but does not report language-model exponent or compute-optimal-split sensitivity.

fits_no_version.finding: An additive two-source power law (labeled/unlabeled, or class subsets) used to extrapolate data requirements gives 16-86% target-failure rates across costs and rounds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-source additive power-law learning curves extrapolate data requirements reliably.

record.code_released: no; the paper states the code is proprietary. Project page: https://nv-tlabs.github.io/LearnOptimizeCollect/
record.problems: The empirical collection-policy evaluation is a simulation using piecewise-linear ground-truth approximations built from measured learning curves, rather than repeated end-to-end data-collection experiments. Results use five seeds. The authors note extreme outcomes and remove 99th-percentile cost outliers in multi-source results; the study is limited to computer vision.
record.rows_left_out: Cost-ratio values from Tables 1 and 2 are omitted because they measure collection-cost suboptimality, not the scaling-law prediction of performance or target attainment. LOC outcome values and alternative-regression LOC comparisons (including Table 6) are omitted because they assess the new policy rather than the power-law fit itself.

untested.parts: All: no language-model pretraining loss, and no parameter, token or compute sweeps.
All for language-model loss. The vision analogue (about 10× data extrapolation of accuracy) is recorded under V5.
All: no architecture shape comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer. Model-size or compute scaling in vision: only training-set size is varied, with fixed architectures. Extrapolation beyond about one order of magnitude.
All: no downstream performance vs pretraining scale or loss.
Parameter counting, schedules and compute-optimal split. Fitting-function dependence appears only via Table 6 failure rates, which no row records.

missing.what: Failure rates of alternative regression baselines on CIFAR-100. Logarithmic 43/37/34%, arctan 23/15/12%, algebraic root 52/44/44% vs power law 56/48/48% at T=1/3/5. Extrapolation error depends on the fitted functional form; arctan is the least optimistic.
Histograms of bootstrap D* estimates on CIFAR-100. The mode is far from the true D*, and higher targets give larger underestimates of required data.

record.verdict_notes: Evidence comes from a simulation using piecewise-linear ground-truth curves built from measured subsets, with 5 seeds; Figure 5 is a single seed. The fitted form is the standard saturating power law v = θ0 q^θ1 + θ2, fitted with weighted least squares favouring larger q. Failure rate is an indirect, decision-level proxy for extrapolation error. Values near 50% are consistent with unbiased noise; values near 100% indicate systematic overprediction. The reader's baseline values (LOC failure rates) compare against the study's own method and should be replaced. The reader's V6 links were wrong because no pretraining or downstream relation is measured. Its V7 label lacked linked rows; the relevant fitting-form evidence is Table 6, now listed under missing.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss of language models and its dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of language-model runs orders of magnitude larger from small pretraining runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, including their growth with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
The study tests power-law learning-curve fits in image/vision tasks only. It does not test video, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer learning.

The study tests extrapolation of validation performance/data requirements in vision tasks; it does not test downstream performance as a function of language-model pretraining loss or language-model scale.

The study tests power-law fitting for data-size learning curves and reports prediction failures. It does not test parameter-counting choices, language-model training schedules, or how compute-optimal model/token allocation changes with fitting choices.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Power-law regression learning-curve estimates used to select data requirements; target attainment evaluated in the simulation.
rows.measure: Failure rate of the power-law regression data-requirement estimate
rows.note: Power-law regression baseline; rate is averaged over a range of target V*.
rows.check: The baseline field holds LOC's failure rate (60%). LOC is the study's own method, not a reference for the scaling law; the meaningful reference is 0% failure, i.e. accurate extrapolation. 100% failure at T=1 means the power-law fit from 10% of data always overpredicted accuracy at larger q. That bears on V5 (image models), not V6, which concerns downstream performance vs pretraining scale or loss. The original 'absent' state was set against LOC and is meaningless.

relationships.condition: Power law fitted to first 10% of data on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, BDD100K, nuScenes (single source)
relationships.reason: Fitted mean curve consistently above measured ground truth (r19-r24). Point extrapolations miss targets 31-100% of the time, near 100% at T=1 on CIFAR-10, ImageNet and nuScenes (r01-r15). The form fits early data but extrapolates optimistically.
relationships.display_finding: Mean extrapolations consistently exceeded measured performance, while point predictions missed targets 31–100% of the time, approaching 100% at T = 1 on CIFAR-10, ImageNet and nuScenes.

relationships.reason: Power-law extrapolation met targets in most instances (failure 36%, 8%, 6% at T=1,3,5), so there is no systematic overshoot in this decision metric (r16-r18).
relationships.display_finding: Power-law extrapolation failed to meet targets in 36%, 8%, and 6% of instances at T = 1, 3, and 5, respectively.
